name: Real-time analytics serving
description: The lean real-time stack: events flow through a broker straight into a real-time OLAP store that ingests continuously and answers analytical queries in milliseconds, with dashboards or product APIs reading directly on top. Unlike Kappa (5), there is no heavy stream-processing layer — the OLAP engine's ingest-time transforms and materialized views do the light shaping, which keeps the moving-part count low. This is the shape behind ops dashboards that update live, usage meters, and analytics APIs embedded in products, where 'the data is 20 minutes old' is a bug report.
when_to_use: Choose this when queries must be answered in under a second over data that is seconds old — live operational monitoring, usage/billing meters, customer-facing analytics endpoints — and when the transformations needed at ingest are light (parsing, filtering, simple enrichment).
It is the fastest path to real-time value because it skips the stream-processing engine entirely.
Users expect dashboards that move as events happen, not on refresh.
when_not_to_use: Skip it when freshness requirements are minutes-or-more — a warehouse with frequent micro-batches is cheaper and simpler.
If ingest requires heavy stateful transformation (multi-stream joins, sessionization), you are actually building Kappa (5) and should add Flink deliberately.
Real-time OLAP stores are also poor system-of-record databases — keep the durable history in the lake or warehouse.

hot_spots.title: Ingest hiccups
hot_spots.detail: A consumer stall shows up as frozen dashboards and erodes trust fast.

hot_spots.title: Query concurrency
hot_spots.detail: Sub-second SLAs collapse when dashboard fan-out overwhelms the store.

hot_spots.title: Late events
hot_spots.detail: Out-of-order arrivals silently understate the most recent windows.

stages.name: Stream
stages.role: Buffer events between producers and the OLAP store; absorb ingest spikes
stages.rationale: Kafka decouples producers from the store, absorbs bursts, and lets you re-ingest after schema or table changes — and every real-time OLAP engine's best-supported ingest path is its Kafka consumer. Redpanda is the lower-ops drop-in; Kinesis and Pub/Sub fit cloud-native estates where a managed service outweighs ecosystem breadth. Skipping the broker and writing directly to the store is tempting but costs you replay and burst protection — usually a false economy.

stages.name: Raw archive
stages.role: Parallel raw sink for backfills and reprocessing without replaying producers
stages.rationale: Cheap immutable object storage as the landing layer decouples ingestion from processing: replays, backfills, and audits read the raw dump instead of re-extracting from sources.

stages.name: OLAP
stages.role: Continuously ingest from the stream and serve sub-second analytical queries
stages.rationale: ClickHouse is the pragmatic default: exceptional scan speed, materialized views for ingest-time shaping, rich SQL, modest operational footprint for a single-node start, and a managed cloud when you outgrow it. Its watch-outs are high-concurrency point lookups and heavy joins — design tables around the queries. Pinot overtakes it for user-facing workloads at thousands of QPS thanks to purpose-built indexes; Druid is the mature incumbent in the same seat; StarRocks when you cannot denormalize and need real-time joins; QuestDB when the workload is narrowly time-series metrics.

stages.name: API/BI
stages.role: Expose the store: live dashboards for humans, HTTP endpoints for products — the doc's 'custom' API half is your own service code
stages.rationale: Grafana's auto-refreshing, time-series-native dashboards are the natural front end for live operational views, with solid ClickHouse and Pinot plugins. For the product-API half there is no corpus tool to buy — a thin service of parameterized, allow-listed queries in your app stack is the right build, and Cube earns a place as the semantic/caching/row-level-security layer under it when many endpoints share definitions (see blueprint 22). Superset or Metabase fit when consumers want exploratory BI rather than ops dashboards.
